title: High-Rate Quantum Codes with Proven Distance and Low-Weight Measurements
authors: Kishor Bharti, Tobias Haug, Runzhou Tao, Kevin Ye
abstract: We study a family of quantum subsystem codes defined on rectangular coordinate grids of any dimension, with even side lengths of at least four. The directly measured operators act along coordinate lines. For every member of the family, we derive the number of protected logical qubits and prove its dressed distance without a numerical search. To illustrate the resulting design choices, we impose a budget of at most 10,000 data qubits and determine the complete tradeoff between encoding rate and measurement weight within this family at distances 16, 32, and 64. At distance 16, one code protects 4,096 logical qubits among 10,000 data qubits using weight-ten measurements. At distances 32 and 64, codes with 7,776 and 9,216 data qubits protect 1,024 and 256 logical qubits, respectively, using weight-six measurements. We include and explain Lean code snippets throughout the paper to guide readers through the formal verification of our subsystem-code construction and its dressed and bare distances.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous theory for a specific family of quantum error-correcting codes defined on rectangular grids. It mathematically proves the exact distance of these codes and, crucially, maps out the achievable trade-off between the encoding rate and the required measurement weight. This provides concrete, constructive blueprints for building resource-efficient quantum memory.
main_problem: To find a useful finite construction for quantum error correction that explicitly relates the protected capacity (encoding rate), the minimum support of an undetectable logical Pauli error (distance), and the weight of the measured operators (measurement weight).
main_result: The authors derive explicit formulas for a family of subsystem codes on rectangular grids, proving the dressed distance is exactly $2L$ (twice the number of dimensions) and establishing a concrete, constructive tradeoff between encoding rate and measurement weight.
method: The analysis uses algebraic techniques involving quotient spaces over F2, formal verification via Lean code snippets, and finite-rate optimization to map out the rate-weight frontier.
model_or_system: The study focuses on a family of quantum subsystem codes defined on rectangular coordinate grids of any dimension, with even side lengths of at least four. These codes are of the Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) type.
key_observables: Encoding Rate ($K/N$), Dressed Distance ($D$), Measurement Weight ($w$), and the number of protected logical qubits ($K$).
important_parameters: The side lengths $q_1, \dots, q_L$ (must be even and $\ge 4$), the total data qubits $N$, and the budget constraint (e.g., $N \le 10,000$).
main_assumptions: The derived parameters are for a specific family of codes, and the analysis relies on formal proofs regarding the full-center equality and the structure of the gauge group.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the supports of gauge operators and logical operators in small examples (e.g., $4 	imes 4$ code), and the main results are summarized in tables showing the rate-weight frontiers for fixed distances (D=16, 32, 64).
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the code structure on rectangular grids, deriving the exact distance using quotient space arguments, and finally performing a finite, explicit enumeration to map the optimal rate-weight trade-off for fixed distances.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, mathematically verifiable constructions for QEC codes, which is foundational for building fault-tolerant quantum computation architectures, linking abstract algebraic structures to physical resource constraints.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three supports in the 4 × 4 code. (a) A row and a column meet once, so the indicated opposite-Pauli gauge operators anticommute. Each has weight four. (b) The four highlighted sites support a minimum logical operator. (c) Two parallel rows support a weight-eight stabilizer. The colors specify supports; panels (b) and (c) can be used in either pure Pauli sector.

Figure 2: Exact rate–weight frontiers at fixed distance under 10,000 data qubits. The points are the discrete choices in Table 1; line segments guide the eye and do not represent intermediate codes. Increasing the number of axes raises distance and reduces the maximum achievable rate under this budget.
